div.head: SUBSECT. 2.
How love tyrannizeth over men. Love, or Heroical melancholy his definition, part affected.
div.p: You have heard how this tyrant Love rageth with Brute beasts and spirits; now let us consider what passions it causeth amongst men.

l.hi: Improbe amor quid non mortalia pectora cogis?

lg.l: [Cruel love, to what do you not drive mortal hearts?]

div.p: How it tickles the hearts of mortal men,

lg.l: Horresco referens, ———
[I shudder to mention it …]

div.p:
I am almost afraid to relate, amazed, For it is a shame to speak of those things which are done of them in secret, Eph. 5. 12.and ashamed, it hath wrought such stupend and prodigious effects, such foul offences. Love indeed (I may not deny) first united Provinces, built Cities, and by a perpetual generation makes and preserves mankind, propagates the Church; but if it rage it is no more love, but burning lust, a disease, Frenzy, Madness, Hell. Plutarch. amator. lib.Est orcus ille, vis est immedicabilis, est rabies insana [It is a hell, an incurable compulsion, a raving madness]; ’tis no virtuous habit this, but a vehement perturbation of the mind, a monster of nature, wit, and art, as Alexis in Lib. 13.Athenaeus sets it out, viriliter audax, muliebriter timidum, furore praeceps, labore infractum, mel felleum, blanda percussio, &c. [manfully daring, womanishly timid, rash in fury, unbroken by exertion, bitter honey, a pleasurable beating, etc.] It subverts kingdoms, overthrows cities, towns, families, mars, corrupts, and makes a massacre of men; thunder and lightning, wars, fires, plagues, have not done that mischief to mankind, as this burning lust, this brutish passion. Let Sodom and Gomorrah, Troy (which Dares Phrygius, and Dictis Cretensis will make good), and
I know not how many cities bear record, ——— & fuit ante Helenam [and before Helen’s time], &c., all succeeding ages will subscribe: Joan of Naples in Italy, Fredegund and Brunehaut in France, all histories are full of these Basilisks. Besides those daily monomachies, murders, effusion of blood, rapes, riot and immoderate expense, to satisfy their lusts, beggary, shame, loss, torture, punishment, disgrace, loathsome diseases that proceed from thence, worse than calentures and pestilent fevers, those often Gouts, Pox, Arthritis, palsies, cramps, Sciatica, convulsions, aches, combustions, &c., which torment the body, that feral melancholy which crucifies the Soul in this life, and everlastingly torments in the world to come.

Notwithstanding they know these and many such miseries, threats, tortures will surely come upon them, rewards, exhortations, e contra; yet either out of their own weakness, a depraved nature, or love’s tyranny, which so furiously rageth, they suffer themselves to be led like an ox to the slaughter; facilis descensus Averni [the descent to hell is easy], they go down headlong to their own perdition, they will commit folly with beasts, men leaving the natural use of women, as Rom. 1. 27.Paul saith, burned in lust one towards another, and man with man wrought filthiness.

Semiramis equo, Pasiphae tauro, Aristo Ephesius asinae se commiscuit, Fulvius equae, alii canibus, capris, &c., unde monstra nascuntur aliquando, Centauri, Sylvani, & ad terrorem hominum prodigiosa spectra: nec cum brutis, sed ipsis hominibus rem habent, quod peccatum Sodomiae vulgo dicitur; & frequens olim vitium apud Orientales illos fuit, Graecos nimirum, Italos, Afros, Asianos: Lilius Giraldus vita ejus.Hercules Hylam habuit, Polycletum, Dionem, Perithoonta, Abderum & Phryga; alii & Euristium ab Hercule amatum tradunt. Pueros amare solis Philosophis relinquendum vult, Lucianus dial. Amorum.Socrates pulchrorum Adolescentum causa frequens Gymnasium obibat, flagitiosoque spectaculo pascebat oculos, quod & Philebus & Phaedon, Rivales, Charmides & reliqui Platonis Dialogi, satis superque testatum faciunt: quod vero Alcibiades de eodem Socrate loquatur, lubens conticesco, sed & abhorreo; tantum incitamentum praebet libidini. At hunc perstrinxit Theodoretus lib. de curat. graec. affect. cap. ultimo. Quin & ipse Plato suum demiratur Agathonem, Xenophon Cliniam, Virgilius Alexin, Anacreon Bathyllum; quod autem de Nerone, Claudio, caeterorumque portentosa libidine memoriae proditum, mallem a Petronio, Suetonio, caeterisque petatis, quando omnem fidem excedat, quam a me expectetis; sed vetera querimur. Busbequius.Apud Asianos, Turcas, Italos, nunquam frequentius hoc quam hodierno die vitium; Diana Romanorum Sodomia: officinae horum alicubi apud Turcas,

arenas arantes; & frequentes querelae, etiam inter ipsos conjuges hac de re, quae virorum concubitum illicitum calceo in oppositam partem verso magistratui indicant; nullum apud Italos familiare magis peccatum, qui & post Lucianus Charidemo.Lucianum & Achilles Tatius lib. 2.
Tatium, scriptis voluminibus defendunt. Johannes de la Casa, Beneventinus Episcopus, divinum opus vocat, suave scelus, adeoque jactat se non alia usum Venere. Nihil usitatius apud monachos, Cardinales, sacrificulos, etiam Non est haec mentula demens. Mart.furor hic ad mortem, ad insaniam. Jovius Musc.Angelus Politianus, ob pueri amorem, violentas sibi manus injecit. Et horrendum sane dictu, quantum apud nos patrum memoria, scelus detestandum hoc saevierit! Quum enim Anno 1538, prudentissimus Rex Henricus Octavus cucullatorum coenobia, & sacrificorum collegia, votariorum, per venerabiles legum Doctores Thomam Leum, Richardum Laytonum visitari fecerat, &c., tanto numero reperti sunt apud eos scortatores, cinaedi, ganeones, paedicones, puerarii, paederastae, Sodomitae (Praefat. lectori lib. de vitiis pontif.Balei verbis utor), Ganimedes, &c., ut in unoquoque eorum novam credideris Gomorrham. Sed vide si lubet eorundem Catalogum apud eundem Baleum; puellae (inquit) in lectis dormire non poterant ob fratres necromanticos. Haec si apud votarios, monachos, sanctos scilicet homiunciones, quid in foro, quid in aula factum suspiceris? Quid apud nobiles, quid inter fornices, quam non foeditatem, quam non spurcitiem? Sileo interim turpes illas, & ne nominandas quidem monachorum Mercurialis cap. de Priapismo. Caelius lib. 11 antiq. lect. cap. 14. Galenus 6 de locis aff.mastrupationes, mastubatores De morb. mulier. lib. 1 cap. 15.Rodericus à Castro vocat, tum & eos qui se invicem ad Venerem excitandam flagris caedunt, Spintrias, Succubas, Ambubeias, & lasciviente lumbo Tribades illas mulierculas, quae se invicem fricant, & praeter Eunuchos etiam ad Venerem explendam, artificiosa illa veretra habent. Immo quod magis mirere, foemina foeminam Constantinopoli non ita pridem deperiit, ausa rem plane incredibilem, mutato cultu mentita virum de nuptiis sermonem init, & brevi nupta est: sed authorem ipsum consule, Busbequium. Omitto Herodotus lib. 2 Euterpe: Uxores insignium virorum non statim vita functas tradunt condiendas, ac ne eas quidem foeminas quae formosae sunt, sed quatriduo ante defunctas, ne cum iis salinarii concumbant, &c.Salinarios illos Aegyptiacos, qui cum formosarum cadaveribus concumbunt; & eorum vesanam libidinem, qui etiam idola & imagines depereunt. Nota est fabula Pigmalionis apud Metamor. 10.Ovidium; Mundi & Paulini apud Aegesippum belli Jud. lib. 2 cap. 4, Pontius C. Caesaris legatus, referente Plinio, lib. 35 cap. 3, quem suspicor eum esse qui Christum crucifixit, picturis Atalantae & Helenae adeo libidine incensus, ut tollere eas vellet si natura tectorii permisisset, alius statuam bonae Fortunae deperiit (Aelianus lib. 9 cap. 37), alius Bonae deae, & ne qua pars probro vacet. Seneca de ira, lib. 11 cap. 18.Raptus ad stupra (quod ait ille) & ne Nullus est meatus ad quem non pateat aditus impudicitiae. Clemens Alex. paedag. lib. 3 cap. 3.os quidem a libidine exceptum. Heliogabalus per omnia cava corporis libidinem recepit, Lamprid. vita ejus. Seneca 1 nat. quaest.Hostius quidam specula fecit, & ita disposuit, ut quum virum ipse pateretur, aversus omnes admissarii motus in speculo videret, ac deinde falsa magnitudine ipsius membri
tanquam vera gauderet, simul virum & foeminam passus, quod dictu foedum & abominandum. Ut verum plane sit, quod apud Tom. 2 Gryllo.Plutarchum Gryllus Ulyssi objecit. Ad hunc usque diem apud nos neque mas marem, neque foemina foeminam amavit, qualia multa apud vos memorabiles & praeclari viri fecerunt: ut viles missos faciam, Hercules imberbem sectans socium, amicos deseruit, &c. Vestrae libidines intra suos naturae fines coerceri non possunt, quin instar fluvii exundantis atrocem foeditatem, tumultum, confusionemque naturae gignant in re Venerea: nam & capras, porcos, equos inierunt viri & foeminae, insano bestiarum amore exarserunt, unde Minotauri, Centauri, Sylvani, Sphinges, &c. Sed ne confutando doceam, aut ea foras efferam, quae non omnes scire convenit (haec enim doctis solummodo, quod causa non absimili De morbis mulierum lib. 1 cap. 15.Rodericus, scripta velim) ne levissimis ingeniis & depravatis mentibus foedissimi sceleris notitiam, &c., nolo quem diutius hisce sordibus inquinare.

[Semiramis had coitus with a horse, Pasiphae with a bull, Aristo of Ephesus with a she-ass, Fulvius with a mare, others with dogs, goats, etc., from which monsters are sometimes born, Centaurs, Sylvans, and unnatural apparitions that terrify men. They do this not only with wild beasts, but even with other men, which is the sin commonly called sodomy; and this vice was once frequent among Orientals, and doubtless among Greeks, Italians, Africans, and Asiatics. Hercules had Hylas, Polycletus, Dion, Perithoas, Abderus and Phryga; others suggest that he was the lover of Eurystheus. He wants the love of boys to be permitted only for philosophers. {Lucian}Socrates often visited the gymnasium because of the beautiful young men, feeding his eyes on the shameful sight, which is confirmed well enough, and more, by the Philebus and Phaedo, the Rivals, Charmides, and the rest of Plato’s Dialogues; indeed, Alcibiades said of the same Socrates, ‘I’d willingly keep silent, but don’t want to, he offers such an incitement to lust.’ Theodoret censures this in the last chapter of his book On the Cure of the Greek Maladies. Plato himself, moreover, marvels at his Agathon, Xenophon his Cleinias, Virgil his Alexis, Anacreon his Bathyllus. For what is recorded of Nero, Claudius and the revolting lusts of the others, however, rather than expecting it from me, I would prefer you to go to Petronius, Suetonius, and the rest, as this goes beyond all credibility; but I lament ancient evils. Among the Asians, Turks and Italians, this vice has never been more common than it is today. Sodomy is the Diana of the Romans; somewhere among the Turks there’s a workshop for these people

lg.l: … who sow their seed in the rocks …

div.p:
ploughing the sands, and frequent quarrels even among the married about this, ‘when wives reveal their husbands’ illicit sex to the magistrate by turning their shoes around the wrong way’; no sin is more familiar among the Italians, who following Lucian and Achilles Tatius, defend it in voluminous writings. Giovanni della Casa, bishop of Benevento, calls it a divine work, a sweet crime, and even boasts that he doesn’t practise any other kind of sex. Nothing is more common among monks, cardinals, priests; this is a Isn’t this prick insane? {Martial}raging desire even to
madness and death. Angelo Poliziano laid violent hands on himself, because of the love of boys. And it is truly horrible to say how much, within the memory of our fathers, this execrable crime has raged among us! For when ‘in the year 1538 the most wise King Henry VIII caused the monks’ cloisters and the colleges of priests and votaries to be inspected by the venerable doctors of laws Thomas Legh and Richard Layton, there were discovered in them such a great number of fornicators, catamites, sensualists, buggerers, boy-lovers, pederasts, sodomites’ (I use the words of Bale), ‘Ganymedes, etc., that in each of them you’d think you were in a new Gomorrah’. But look if you like at the catalogue of these people in the same Bale; ‘novice nuns’ (he says) ‘were unable to sleep in their beds because of necromantic friars’. If this was how it was among votaries, monks and men who were evidently little saints, what do you think was done in the marketplace or at court, among nobles or in brothels, that isn’t filthy or obscene? Meanwhile I’m keeping silent about such repulsive and unnameable acts as the onanism of monks (‘masturbators’, Rodrigo de Castro calls them), and about those who take turns to beat themselves for erotic excitement with whips, and about rent boys, sluts and courtesans, and those silly lesbians with lascivious loins who frig each other, and even eunuchs who have those artificial penises to satisfy their lust. Indeed, even more astonishingly, not long ago a woman in Constantinople was dying with love for another woman, and dared to do something completely incredible: after changing her clothing she went through the wedding ceremony pretending to be a man, and in brief was married; but consult the author himself, Busbequius. I say nothing of those They don’t deliver the dead bodies of the wives of distinguished men to be embalmed immediately, nor also those of beautiful women, but only after they’ve been dead for four days, so that the embalmers don’t have intercourse with them, etc. {Herodotus}Egyptian embalmers who lie with the corpses of beautiful women, or of the raging lust of those who fall desperately in love with visions and pictures. The story of Pygmalion in Ovid is well known; that of Mundus and Paulina in Hegesippus, The Jewish War Bk 2 ch. 4, Pontius the legate of Gaius Caesar, mentioned by Pliny, Bk 35 ch. 3, whom I suspect to be the man who crucified Christ, was so inflamed with lust by paintings of Atalanta and Helena that he wanted to take them away with him, if only the nature of the plasterwork had allowed it; another man madly loved the statue of Bona Fortuna (Aelian, Bk 9 ch. 37), and another that of Bona Dea; and no part of the body can keep free from lewdness – ‘abductions for rape’ (as {Seneca} says), ‘and not even the mouth is exempt from lust’. Heliogabalus admitted pleasure by every There’s no pathway that’s inaccessible to lasciviousness. {Clement of Alexandria}orifice of the body, according to Lampridius in his Life. Someone called Hostius constructed a {magnifying} mirror and arranged it in such a way that, when he was submitting to a another man’s lust, he could see all the movement of his stallion behind in the mirror, and then he would delight in the deceptive size of his partner’s member as if it were real, and in prostituting himself to a man and a woman at the same time – which is horrible and detestable to mention. So it’s clearly true, as Gryllus reproached Ulysses in Plutarch: ‘To this day among us neither has a male loved a male, nor a female a female – things that many of your remarkable and famous men have done (not to mention the
common people): Hercules deserted his friends to pursue a beardless, etc. Your lusts can’t be contained within their natural limits; instead, in matters of love, like overflowing rivers they bring forth hideous filthiness, agitation, and confusion to nature; for men have penetrated goats, pigs and horses, and women have burned with insane love for beasts, the result being Minotaurs, Centaurs, Sylvans, Sphinxes, etc.’ But in case by condemning them I teach or spread abroad these things, which are not appropriate for everyone to know (for, like Rodericus, I would prefer them to be written down only for the learned), and in case the really dim-witted and depraved minds should gain knowledge of the vilest crimes, etc., I’m unwilling to contaminate anyone with this filth for any longer.]

I come at last to that Heroical Love, which is proper to men and women, is a frequent cause of melancholy, and deserves much rather to be called burning lust, than by such an honourable title. There is an honest love I confess, which is natural, laqueus occultus captivans corda hominum, ut a mulieribus non possint separari, a secret snare to captivate the hearts of men [so that they can’t be parted from women], as Amphitheat. amor. cap. 4 interpret. Curtio.Christopher Fonseca proves, a strong allurement, of a most attractive, occult, adamantine property, and powerful virtue, and no man living can avoid it. Aeneas Silvius.Et qui vim non sensit amoris, aut lapis est, aut bellua [And he who hasn’t felt the power of love is either a rock or a wild beast]. He is not a man but a block, a very stone, aut Numen, aut Nebuchadnezzar [either a god or a Nebuchadnezzar], he hath a gourd for his head, a Tertul. proverb. lib. 4 adversus Marc. cap. 40.pepon for his heart, that hath not felt the power of it, and a rare creature to be found, one in an age,

l.hi: Qui nunquam visae flagravit amore puellae:

lg.l: [Who blazed with love for a girl never seen:]

div.p: for semel insanavimus omnes [we’ve all been insane once], dote we either young or old, as Chaucer.he said, and none are excepted but Minerva and the Muses: so Cupid in Tom. 1 dial. deorum Lucianus. Amore non ardent Musae [The Muses aren’t inflamed with love].Lucian complains to his mother Venus, that amongst all the rest, his arrows could not pierce them. But this nuptial love, is a common passion, an honest, for men to love in the way of marriage; ut materia appetit formam, sic mulier virum [as matter longs for form, so woman longs for man]. You know marriage is honourable, a blessed calling, appointed by God himself in Paradise, it breeds true peace, tranquillity, content and happiness, qua nulla est aut fuit unquam sanctior conjunctio [than which there is not, and never has been, any holier union], as Daphnaeus in In amator. dialog.Plutarch could well prove, & quae generi humano immortalitatem parat [and which prepares the human race for immortality], when they live without jarring, scolding, lovingly as they should do.

l.hi: Quos irrupta tenet copula, nec ullis

lg.l: Suprema citius solvit amor die.
Thrice happy they, and more than that,
Whom bonds of love so firmly ties,
That without brawls till death them part,
’Tis undissolv’d and never dies.

div.p: As Seneca lived with his Paulina, Abraham and Sarah, Orpheus and Eurydice, Arria and Paetus, Artemisia and Mausolus, Rubenius Celer, that would needs have it engraven on his tomb, he had led his life with Ennia his dear wife forty-three years eight months, and never fell out. There is no pleasure in this world comparable to it, ’tis summum mortalitatis bonum [the highest good of mankind] ——— Lucretius.hominum divumque voluptas, Alma Venus ——— [the delight of men and gods, bountiful Venus …] latet enim in muliere aliquid majus potentiusque omnibus aliis humanis voluptatibus, as Fonseca.one holds, there’s something in a woman beyond all human delight; a magnetic virtue, a charming quality, an occult and powerful motive. The husband rules her as head, but she again commands his heart, he is her servant, she his only joy and content: no happiness is like unto it, no love so great as this of man and wife, no such comfort, as Hor.placens uxor, a sweet wife:

l.hi: Omnis amor magnus, sed aperto in conjuge major,

lg.l: [Every love is great, but greater in an acknowledged spouse,]

div.p: when they love at last as fresh as they did at first,

lg.l: [The beloved woman grows old with a beloved husband,]

div.p: as Homer brings Paris kissing Helena, after they had been married ten years, protesting withal that he loved her as dear as he did the first hour that he was betrothed. And in their old age when they make much of one another, saying as he did to his wife in the Poet,

l.hi: Nec ferat ulla dies ut commutemur in aevo,

lg.l: Quin tibi sim juvenis, tuque puella mihi.
Dear wife, let’s live in love, and die together,
As hitherto we have in all good will:
Let no day change or alter our affections,
But let’s be young to one another still.

div.p: Such should conjugal love be, still the same, and as they are one flesh, so should they be of one mind, as in an Aristocratical government, one consent, Geryon amicitiae symbolum [Geryon, symbol of friendship].Geryon-like, corpus coalescere in unum [grow together as a single body], have one heart in two bodies, will and nill the same. A good wife according to Plutarch, should be as a looking-glass to represent her husband’s face and passion: if he be pleasant, she should be merry: if he laugh, she should smile; if he look sad, she should participate of his sorrow, and bear a part with him, and so they should continue in mutual love one towards another.

l.hi: Et me ab amore tu deducet nulla senectus,

lg.l: Sive ego Tythonus, sive ego Nestor ero.
No age shall part my love from thee sweet wife,
Though I live Nestor or Tithonus’ life.

div.p: And she again to him, as the Plutarch. cap. 30 Rom. hist.Bride saluted the Bridegroom of old in Rome, Ubi tu Gaius, ego semper Gaia, be thou still Gaius, I’ll be Gaia.

’Tis an happy state this indeed, when the fountain is blessed (saith Solomon, Prov. 5. 17) and he rejoiceth with the wife of his youth, and she is to him as the loving Hind, and pleasant Roe, and he delights in her continually. But this love of ours is immoderate, inordinate, and not to be comprehended in any bounds. It will not contain itself within the union of marriage, or apply to one object, but is a wandering, extravagant, a domineering, a boundless, an irrefragable, a destructive passion: sometimes this burning lust rageth after marriage, and then it is properly called Jealousy; sometimes before, and then it is called Heroical melancholy; it extends sometimes to corrivals, &c., begets rapes, incests, murders: Marcus Antoninus compressit Faustinam sororem, Caracalla Juliam Novercam, Nero Matrem, Caligula sorores, Cyneras Mirrham filiam, &c. [Marcus Antoninus had intercourse with his sister Faustina, Caracalla with his stepmother Julia, Nero with his mother, Caligula with his sisters, Cinyras with his daughter Myrrha, etc.] But it is confined within no terms of blood, years, sex, or whatsoever else. Some furiously rage before they come to discretion or age. Junonem habeam iratam, si unquam meminerim me virginem fuisse. Infans enim paribus inquinata sum, & subinde majoribus me applicui, donec ad aetatem perveni, ut Milo vitulum, inde taurum, &c. [May I bear the anger of Juno if I recall ever having been a virgin. For as an infant I defiled myself with my companions, and after that I devoted myself to older ones, until I came of age, like Milo: first a calf, then a bull, etc.]Quartilla in Petronius, never remembered she was a maid: and the wife of Bath in Chaucer, cracks,

l.hi: Since I was twelve years old, believe,
Husbands at Kirk door had I five.

div.p: Pornodidasc. dial. lat. interp. Casp. Barthio ex Ital.Aretine’s Lucretia sold her maidenhead a thousand times before she was twenty-four years old, plus millies vendideram virginitatem, &c., neque te celabo, non deerant qui ut integram ambirent [I won’t hide it from you: there was no lack of people after it, as if it were untouched]. Rahab the harlot began to be a professed quean at ten years of age, and was but fifteen when she hid the spies, as Anglico scriptur. concentu.Hugh Broughton proves, to whom Serarius the Jesuit, quaest. 6 in cap. 2 Josue, subscribes. Generally women begin pubescere [to attain puberty] as they call it, or catullire [to be on heat], as Julius Pollux cites, lib. 2 cap. 3 onomast. out of Aristophanes, Epictetus cap. 42. Mulieres statim ab anno 14. movere incipiunt, &c., attrectari se sinunt & exponunt [As soon as they are fourteen, women start to make an impression, etc., allow themselves to be touched and put themselves forward]. Levinus Lemnius.at fourteen years old, then they do offer themselves, and some plainly rage. Lib. 3 fol. 126.Leo Afer saith, that in Africk a man shall scarce find a maid at fourteen years of age, they are so forward, and many amongst us after they come into the teens do not live without husbands, but linger. What pranks in this kind the middle age have played, is not to be recorded.

l.hi: Si mihi sint centum linguae, sint oraque centum,

lg.l: [If I had a hundred tongues, and a hundred mouths,]

div.p: no tongue can sufficiently declare, every story is full of men and women’s unsatiable lust, Nero’s, Heliogabali, Bonosi, &c. Catullus.Caelius Auphilenum, sed Quintius Auphelinam depereunt, &c. [Caelius is desperate for Aufillenus, and Quintius for Aufillena, etc.] They neigh after other men’s wives (as Jeremy cap. 5. 8 complaineth) like fed horses, or range like town Bulls, raptores virginum & viduarum [ravishers of virgins and widows], as many of our great ones do. Solomon’s wisdom was extinguished in this fire of lust, Samson’s strength enervated, piety in Lot’s daughters quite forgot, gravity of Priesthood in Eli’s sons, reverend old age in the Elders that would violate Susanna, filial duty in Absalom to his stepmother, brotherly love in Amnon towards his sister. Human, divine laws, precepts, exhortations, fear of God and men, fair, foul means, fame, fortunes, shame, disgrace, honour cannot oppose, stave off, or withstand the fury of it, omnia vincit amor, &c. [love conquers all, etc.] No cord, nor cable can so forcibly draw, or hold so fast, as love can do with a twined thread; the scorching beams under the Equinoctial, or extremity of cold within the circle Arctic, where the very Seas are frozen, cold or torrid zone cannot avoid, or expel this heat, fury and rage of mortal men.

l.hi: Quo fugis ah demens, nulla est fuga, tu licet usque

lg.l: Ad Tanaim fugias, usque sequetur amor.
[Oh, where are you fleeing, you fool? There’s no escape:
Even if you flee to Tanais, love will follow you there.]

div.p: Of women’s unnatural, De mulierum inexhausta libidine luxuque insatiabili omnes aeque regiones conqueri posse existimo [I reckon that all parts of the world can complain equally about the inexhaustible lust and insatiable debauchery of women]. Stephanus.unsatiable lust, what Country, what Village doth not complain? Mother and daughter sometimes dote on the same man, father and son, master and servant on one woman.

lg.l: ——— Sed amor, sed effrenata libido,

l.hi: Quid castum in terris intentatumque reliquit?

lg.l: [… But love, but unbridled lust,
What has it left pure and untouched on earth?]

div.p: What breach of vows and oaths, fury, dotage, madness, might I reckon up? Yet this is more tolerable in youth, and such as are still in their hot blood; but for an old fool to dote, to see an old lecher, what more odious, what can be more absurd? And yet what so common? Who so furious?

l.hi: Amare ea aetate si occeperint, multo insaniunt acrius,

lg.l: [If they start to fall in love at that age, they rave much more violently,]

div.p: some dote then more than ever they did in their youth. How many decrepit, hoary, harsh, writhen, bursten-bellied, toothless, bald, blear-eyed, impotent, rotten, old men shall you see flickering still in every place? One gets him a young wife, another a Courtesan, and when he can scarce lift his leg over a sill, and hath one foot already in Charon’s boat, when he hath the trembling in his joints, the gout in his feet; a perpetual rheum in his head, a continuate cough, Cyprian.his sight fails him, thick of hearing, his breath stinks, all his moisture is dried up and gone, may not spit from him, a very child again, that cannot dress himself, or cut his own meat, yet he will be dreaming of, and honing after wenches, what can be more unseemly? Worse it is in women than in men, when she is aetate declivis, diu vidua, mater olim, parum decore matrimonium sequi videtur, an old widow, a mother so long since (Lib. 8 epist. Ruffinus.in Pliny’s opinion), she doth very unseemly seek to marry, yet whilst she is Hiatque turpis inter aridas nates podex [And a filthy anus gapes between withered buttocks].so old a crone, a beldam, she can neither see, nor hear, nor go stand, a mere Cadaverosa adeo ut ab inferis reversa videri possit, vult adhuc catullire [So cadaverous that she might appear to have returned from the dead, and she still wants intercourse]. Erasmus mor.carcass, a witch, and scarce feel; she caterwauls, and must have a stallion, a Champion, she must and will marry again, and betroth herself to some young man, Nam & matrimoniis est despectum senium [For even in marriage old age is despicable]. Aeneas Silvius.that hates to look on, but for her goods; abhors the sight of her, to the prejudice of her good name, her own undoing, grief of friends, and ruin of her children.

But to enlarge or illustrate this power and effects of love, is to set a candle in
the Sun. Quid toto terrarum orbe communius? Quae civitas, quod oppidum, quae familia vacat amatorum exemplis? [What’s more common in the whole of the world? What state, what town, what family doesn’t contain examples of lovers?] Aeneas Silvius. Quis trigesimum annum natus nullum amoris causa peregit insigne facinus, ego de me facio conjecturam quem amor in mille pericula misit [Who has reached their thirtieth year without accomplishing a remarkable deed for the sake of love? I draw this inference from myself, whom love cast into a thousand perils].It rageth with all sorts and conditions of men, yet is most evident among such as are young and lusty, in the flower of their years, nobly descended, high-fed, such as live idly, and at ease; and for that cause (which our Divines call burning lust) this Forestus, Plato.ferinus, insanus amor, this mad and beastly passion, as I have said, is named by our Physicians, Heroical love, and a more honourable title put upon it, Amor nobilis, as Pract. major. Tract. 6 cap. 1 Rub. 11 de aegrit. capt. Quod his multum contingat [Because it affects many of these people].Savonarola styles it, because noblemen and women make a common practice of it, and are so ordinarily affected with it. Avicenna lib. 3 Fen 1 tract. 4 cap. 23 calleth this passion Ilishi, and defines it to be a disease or melancholy vexation, or anguish of mind, in which a man continually meditates of the beauty, gesture, manners of his Mistress, and troubles himself about it: desiring (as Savonarola adds) with all intentions and eagerness of mind to compass or enjoy her, as commonly Hunters trouble themselves about their sports, the covetous, about their gold & goods, so is he tormented still about his Mistress. Arnaldus Villanovanus in his book of Heroical love defines it, a continual cogitation of that which he desires, with a confidence or hope of compassing it: which definition his Commentator cavils at. For continual cogitation is not the genus, but a symptom of love; we continually think of that which we hate and abhor, as well as that which we love; and many things we covet and desire, without all hope of attaining. Carolus à Lorme in his Questions makes a doubt, an amor sit morbus, whether this heroical love be a disease: Julius Pollux Onomast. lib. 6 cap. 44 determines it; they that are in love are likewise sick; lascivus, salax, lasciviens, & qui in venerem furit, vere est aegrotus [the lascivious man, the salacious man, the lusting man, he who rages in love, is truly diseased]. Arnaldus will have it improperly so called, and a malady rather of the body, than mind. Tully in his Tusculans defines it a furious disease of the mind, Plato madness itself, Ficinus his Commentator, cap. 12, a species of madness, for many have run mad for women, Esdr. 4. 26, but Rhasis a melancholy passion, and most Physicians make it a species, or kind of melancholy (as will appear by the Symptoms) and treat of it apart: whom I mean to imitate, and to discuss it in all his kinds, to examine his several causes, to show his symptoms, indications, prognostics, effects, that so it may be with more facility cured.

The part affected in the meantime, as Arnaldus supposeth, is the former part of the head for want of moisture, which his Commentator rejects. Langius med. epist. lib. 1 cap. 24 will have this passion sited in the liver, and to keep residence in the heart, to proceed first from the eyes so carried by our spirits, and kindled with imagination in the liver and heart; cogit amare jecur [the liver compels love], as the saying is. Medium ferit per epar [It strikes right through the liver],
as Cupid in Anacreon. For some such cause belike Odyss. & Metamor. 4 Ovid.Homer feigns Tityus’ liver (who was enamoured on Latona) to be still gnawed by two Vultures day and night in hell, for that young men’s bowels thus enamoured, are so continually tormented by love. Gordonius cap. 2 part. 2 will have the testicles an immediate subject or cause, the liver an Antecedent. Fracastorius agrees in this with Gordonius, inde primitus imaginatio venerea, erectio, &c., titillatissimam partem vocat, ita ut nisi extruso semine gestiens voluptas non cessat, nec assidua veneris recordatio, addit [from which place, originally, are lustful imagination, erection, etc.; he calls this part the most titillating, so that until semen is ejaculated the pleasure of desiring does not cease, nor the continual awareness of sex, adds] Guastavinius Comment. 4 Sect. prob. 27 Arist. But properly it is a passion of the brain, as all other melancholy, by reason of corrupt imagination, and so doth Jason Pratensis cap. 19 de morb. cerebri (who writes copiously of this Erotical love), place and reckon it amongst the affections of the brain. Cap. de affectibus.Melanchthon de anima confutes those that make the liver a part affected, and Guainerius Tract. 15 cap. 13 & 17, though many put all the affections in the heart, refers it to the brain. Ficinus cap. 7 in Convivium Platonis, will have the Est in sanguine melancholico hujusmodi aestus [There is a boiling of this kind in melancholic blood].blood to be the part affected. Jo. Freitagius cap. 14 noct. med. supposeth all four affected, heart, liver, brain, blood; but the major part concur upon the brain, Est corruptio imaginativae & aestimativae facultatis, ob formam fortiter affixam, corruptumque judicium, ut semper de eo cogitet, ideoque recte melancholicus appellatur [It is a corruption of the imaginative and estimative faculty, by reason of a firmly fixed image and faulty judgement {in that faculty}, so that he is always thinking about it; and therefore it is correctly called melancholic]. Concupiscentia vehemens ex corrupto judicio aestimativae virtutis [Ardent desire arising from the corrupt judgement of the estimative power].’tis imaginatio laesa [damaged imagination]; and both imagination and reason are misaffected; because of his corrupt judgement, and continual meditation of that which he desires, he may truly be said to be melancholy. If it be violent, or his disease inveterate, as I have determined in the precedent partitions, both imagination and reason are misaffected, first one, then the other.
